I’m a dyslexic CEO and every decision I sign off on starts with a pile of documents.

Contracts, legal, finance and more and as CEO you have the last call on all of it.

For the past years of building companies pre-AI, reading was the tax I had to pay before I could do my actual job.

But finally, with AI, that tax has been removed.

A complex contract I’d never volunteer to read, I now get into fast, ask the right questions, delegate and move on. 

On reading, AI can take me to average.

But average is all I need because the hours I used to spend fighting text now go to what I’m actually good at: seeing patterns, connecting people and ideas fast.

AI didn’t take my job. It just took tasks and made me better at the job.

And to be honest I feel the AI debate is so stuck on which jobs disappear but I think the bigger question is which tasks are hiding people’s strengths today.

Some companies are already learning this the expensive way. In a survey, 32% of US hiring managers whose companies cut roles because of AI later had to bring the same or similar roles back.

The most common reason: the work needed knowledge and context AI couldn’t replace.

They cut a job when AI had only taken a task.

Software engineers now represent 55 percent of all Big Tech hires, up from 46 percent in 2019, even as the sector announced more than 165,000 job cuts through September 2026 according to Challenger, Gray & Christmas. SignalFire's 2026 workforce analysis shows overall tech-major hiring fell 25 percent versus 2019, yet engineering hiring dropped only 11 percent, concentrating gains in senior and AI-adjacent roles. The market didn't contract—it moved upstairs, with 71 percent of the 2025-2026 posting rebound coming from senior positions per Indeed Hiring Lab, while new-grad hiring at major firms plummeted roughly 65 percent since 2019.

This bifurcation runs deeper than seniority. Indeed Hiring Lab's July 2025 index shows machine learning engineer openings at 159 percent of their February 2020 baseline while general software engineering listings sit at 51 percent. Frontend, mobile, and legacy stack roles have fallen more than 60 percent from pre-pandemic levels. Meanwhile the AI skill premium has widened to 43 percent for engineers with multiple AI specializations, per SignalFire. Non-tech firms are absorbing displaced talent too—55 percent of non-tech organizations surveyed by CNBC in October 2026 said they were recruiting following tech-sector layoffs, often paying above-market rates for cloud infrastructure, platform engineering, and security expertise that AI tooling cannot yet replace.

For engineers, the move upstairs means optimizing for depth over breadth. Prioritize production-grade AI and ML integration experience over tutorial projects; the premium attaches to engineers who ship models in constrained environments, not those who prompt them. Build visible expertise in cloud-native infrastructure, observability, or security—domains where architectural judgment compounds and AI assistance hits hard limits. For recruiters, stop screening for years of experience in decaying stacks. Rewrite requisitions around verified production outcomes: shipped a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline serving 10K daily queries beats five years of Python. Source from the mid-market and non-tech firms now hiring aggressively; they hold the senior talent Big Tech shed.

Anthropic is HIRING for the discipline most enterprises have yet to fund.
The role is Strategic Finance Lead, Compute. The scope: unit economics of individual training runs. Bottoms-up models of the accelerator fleet. ROI across run size, chip type and data. Compute contracts and pricing structures. Ownership of the source of truth and the plan of record. New frameworks for profitability and capital efficiency.

That is Technology Econometrics, written as a job description.
Anthropic is staffing a dedicated economics function for technology spend, owned by Finance, grounded in unit economics and built to inform capital decisions. It is the right hire.

Every enterprise running AI in production carries the same question at a different scale. What does this workflow cost, fully loaded, per accepted outcome? What does it produce? What happens to the return when usage, pricing, rates or the vendor shift? Which investment clears at P50 and still holds at the P90 cost?

Most enterprises record spend at close, weeks after the cost was incurred, and record value in a separate business case that no one reconciles to execution.

Closing that gap is a build-versus-buy decision, and the visible cost is only the first line. The posted range is $240K to $325K a year for one seat. Over three years, that is $720K to $975K in base salary alone.

The posting names the instruments: budgeting, monthly forecasting, variance analysis, Pigment, SQL, Python and Excel. That stack reads spend after the bill. Unit economics per training run and ROI by chip type require real-time runtime data, so the function depends on engineering to build the pipelines, platform teams to instrument production, and compute, storage and senior time, all absorbed internally. A frontier lab can carry that inside its own resources. Most enterprises cannot.

We knew one finance seat could not build this. ÆTHUX assembled a team: mathematicians, econometricians, econometrics and portfolio trading quants from international banks and Wall Street, CFO-level finance leaders and data engineers.

That team built this capability as a deterministic platform. Atlas establishes a real-time runtime economic baseline on the estate the enterprise already runs, mess included, with no rebuilt systems or pipelines. It computes fully loaded economics per transaction, workflow, inference and outcome, with 162 econometric methods running on that data. Every new workload runs against that baseline before go-live. Deployment to a sealed capital decision runs six to eight weeks. 

Aether prices the capital decision before the capital moves.
Technology is now a production asset on the income statement. The enterprises that govern it with the discipline they already apply to a loan book or a factory floor will set the cost curve for their industries. The discipline has a name, and the market is now hiring for it.

Can software reject a candidate in South Africa?

Section 71 of POPIA says a person may not be subject to a decision that has legal consequences for them, or affects them to a substantial degree, if it is based solely on automated processing of their personal information to profile them. There are exceptions, for example where the decision is made in connection with a contract and appropriate measures protect the person's interests. Those measures include a chance to make representations and enough information about the logic behind the decision.

Why it matters for hiring: a tool that rejects applicants automatically, with no person involved and no explanation, carries risk. A tool that ranks, explains and leaves the decision to a person is a different thing.

That is how Career Screen works: a ranked shortlist, a plain-language reason for every score, and you decide who to interview.

General information, not legal advice. Check your own situation with a qualified attorney.

Source: Bowmans, "South Africa: AI in the workplace (2 of 6): POPIA considerations": https://lnkd.in/erHUat8c

In staging, rate limits feel abstract. You make an API call, wait 800ms, and get a neat response.

Everything changes when you run 20 concurrent multi-agent workflows in production.

A single query triggers a planner spinning up four subagents. Each subagent queries internal tools, fetches docs, and makes multi-turn reasoning calls. Within three seconds, one user interaction creates 40 to 60 downstream requests.

Across enterprise users, downstream systems get crushed:
- Provider TPM and RPM limits trip instantly.
- Frameworks enter blind retry loops, choking memory and queue workers.
- Upstream database connections exhaust, and the pipeline stalls.

Prompt optimization won't solve queue exhaustion. To make high-concurrency agent systems production-ready, engineering teams need a dedicated gateway with three hard boundaries:

1. Token-Bucket Backpressure Gating
Never let worker nodes call external model APIs directly. Route requests through an ingress gateway enforcing token-bucket rate limiting (via Redis or Kafka). When capacity nears 85% of quota ceilings, the gateway applies backpressure—pausing background subagents while prioritizing active user transactions.

2. In-Flight Request Deduplication
In multi-agent loops, subagents often formulate identical embedding lookups or schema queries within the same execution window. The gateway computes deterministic SHA-256 hashes of incoming payloads. If an identical query is in-flight or completed within the last 5 seconds, it serves the cached promise instead of hitting the model twice.

3. Dynamic Multi-Provider Circuit Breakers
Hardcoding a single model provider invites downtime. When 429 rate limits or 5xx timeouts exceed 5% over a rolling 30-second window, the circuit breaker trips. The gateway transparently routes subsequent turns to a secondary failover cluster without aborting session state.

High-concurrency AI isn't an AI problem—it's core distributed systems, queue management, and backend reliability engineering.

The hardest bottleneck Indian engineering teams face building these gateways isn't architecture; it's hiring senior engineering bandwidth fast enough. 

Searching for senior backend and cloud engineers with hands-on Go, Python, Kafka, and Kubernetes experience routinely takes 3 to 4 months due to standard 90-day notice period bottlenecks. That delay stalls critical roadmaps.

At OuterAgentic, we solve this by augmenting enterprise teams with vetted senior contract developers who join your sprints in days, not quarters. Senior engineers ready to handle production-grade backend, cloud, and AI architectures from Day 1.

Tata Consultancy Services says 80% of its business-services contracts are outcome-based. India's IT giants are confronting a new pricing reality.

Indian IT companies grew by hiring more engineers, taking on larger projects, and billing clients for the hours worked.

AI is challenging that equation.
In September 2026, Wipro's CTO revealed that the company's AI initiatives had freed up capacity equivalent to the output of 20,000 employees.

Those employees were redeployed within the company.
Meanwhile, TCS CEO K. Krithivasan told Reuters that roughly 80% of contracts in its finance, HR, and other business services segment are now linked to performance outcomes.

Clients are also demanding cost reductions of 25-30% in some cases.

Consider the implications.
A company once needed a team of engineers to develop, test, maintain, and monitor software.

AI can now automate portions of that work. The client sees higher productivity and expects lower costs. The IT provider still needs to maintain quality, security, and accountability.

For companies building enterprise AI systems, this changes the engineering priorities.
An AI agent may complete a task autonomously. But who verifies its decisions? Who manages exceptions? Who takes responsibility when it fails?

These questions become commercially important when payment depends on results.
TCS, Wipro, Infosys, and Cognizant are navigating an industry where headcount alone can no longer explain the value delivered.

The next competitive advantage could come from building AI systems that businesses trust with measurable outcomes.

Would you pay an IT partner for the engineers assigned or the business results delivered?

GCCs were built to scale headcount. The next chapter will be built on half a pizza.

Two weeks ago I proposed the 𝗛𝗮𝗹𝗳-𝗣𝗶𝘇𝘇𝗮 𝗧𝗲𝗮𝗺: 3 to 4 people, full ownership of one outcome, AI as the rest of the team. https://lnkd.in/p/dFaHvE7T 

Here’s where I think it matters most: Global Capability Centres.

For years, the GCC playbook rewarded size. More seats meant more scope, more budget, more influence with HQ.

AI is quietly rewriting that scorecard.

India now has 2,117 GCCs employing 2.36 million people. But people per centre has started to fall, even as the work moves up the value chain. Centres are being asked to own more with fewer hands.

The math hasn’t changed. A team of 10 carries 45 communication channels. A team of 4 carries 6.

But GCCs carry one more: the channel across time zones. An onshore product owner, an offshore build team, a handoff every night. That one link can cost more than all the others combined.

A comment on my last post sharpened this. Shrink the team, and the slowest link becomes the approval gate. In a GCC, that gate usually sits at HQ, often a continent away.

So the Half-Pizza GCC Team needs two changes at once.

𝗦𝗺𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗺𝘀
1. A product-minded engineer who owns the “why” locally, not through a nightly handoff
2. One or two builders who direct AI rather than out-type it
3. A quality owner who designs guardrails, not test scripts

𝗥𝗶𝘀𝗸-𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀
1. Strict where it touches payments, data or customer contracts
2. Light, or automatic, where it’s an experiment
3. Decided in the centre, not parked until HQ’s morning

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘁 𝗮𝘀𝗸𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗚𝗖𝗖 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗶𝗿 𝗛𝗤 𝘀𝗽𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗼𝗿𝘀:
1. Measure the centre by outcomes owned, not seats filled
2. Move product ownership and approval rights to where the building happens
3. Keep hiring juniors into small teams, where they learn fastest from seniors
4. Build the platform layer so tiny teams can ship without raising tickets

It’s not a headcount cut. The people form more half-pizza teams, each owning a product or platform outright. Same centre. More bets. Fewer handoffs.

𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗰𝗮𝗽𝗮𝗰𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗰𝗮𝗽𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗲. The name was always Global Capability Centre. AI finally lets us live up to it.

The question for every GCC Leader isn’t How many seats will AI take?

It’s How many outcomes does HQ trust us to own?

If you lead a GCC, or sponsor one from HQ, what would stop you trying this?

Is your company scaling headcount faster than it is building the architecture to sustain it?

A few days back, our co-founder Jeenal had a phenomenal experience at the Bengaluru Skill Summit 2026 (Workforce 2030: Scale, Systems, Synergy). 

From debates on assessing skills beyond certificates to sessions on moving from Workforce to Imagination Force highlighting the surge of India’s Orange Economy one truth stood out across every room: 

India doesn’t have a talent or creativity deficit. It has a systems deficit.
Whether you’re scaling a tech startup or an IP-driven creative enterprise, we see the same story unfold every week: founders hire A-players to meet surging demand, only for those teams to stall 90 days later chasing unclear approvals, loose contracts, and broken handoffs.

Placing exceptional minds inside fractured operations doesn't accelerate growth; it manufactures friction.

Three convictions we’re bringing back to our work at Alignix Partners:
- Capability over credentials: Degrees signal potential; clear role design and objective onboarding unlock real performance.
- Clarity precedes automation: Layering AI onto disorganized workflows only scales confusion faster.
- Structure protects creativity: In an imagination-led economy, clean IP agreements, compliance, and governance give teams the freedom to create without chaos.

Grateful to the Department of Skill Development, Entrepreneurship & Livelihood, Government of Karnataka and the speakers for curating conversations that move from policy to real execution. 

A candid thought for fellow builders if you paused all new hiring for 30 days just to audit how your team operates, what is the first structural bottleneck you would uncover?

Building React.js dashboards on top of Python APIs taught me one thing the hard way: the contract between frontend and backend matters more than either side's code.

On my AI Production Incident Investigator, the frontend kept breaking whenever the backend changed a field name or returned a different shape for the same event.

What fixed it:

→ Define the response schema first, then build both sides against it
→ Validate payloads at the API boundary in Python, not in the UI
→ Version endpoints so a change doesn't silently break the React.js views
→ Keep one source of truth for types so both sides stay in sync

The incident feed became far more stable once the API shape stopped drifting. It sounds obvious, but in a full stack project it's the first thing that saves time.

As a full stack engineer working in Australia, I've found this discipline matters even more when teams move quickly. How do you keep frontend and backend contracts in sync on your projects? I'd love to hear what has worked for other engineers and hiring managers.

Global AI companies are hiring in India faster than ever, and it is quietly changing what an Indian tech career looks like.

According to staffing firm Xpheno, tracked for The Economic Times (18 Nov), 24 overseas AI and new-age tech companies now employ around 24,000 people in India. Their combined workforce grew more than 30% in a year.

The list includes Anthropic, OpenAI, ElevenLabs, Perplexity and Replit, alongside Databricks, Figma, Rippling and Glean.

The same report shows the other side of the coin. Indian IT services firms face clients asking for 10–30% discounts on contract renewals in exchange for AI productivity gains (UnearthInsight). And HFS Research says blended token prices fell about 67% between Q1 2025 and Q1 2026, yet 73% of enterprises went over their AI budgets last year.

What I take from this:
→ Product R&D, not just delivery, is moving here. Build skills that ship products.
→ AI savings get shared with the customer. Your value has to sit in judgement, not hours billed.
→ Cheaper tokens don't mean cheaper AI. Whoever governs usage controls cost.

The most expensive assumption in AI strategy for 2026 is that scaling inference compute is the path to better agents.

I have been designing the execution layer for autonomous systems that must act on the world, not just predict it. The latest trends confirm that the bottleneck is no longer model capability. It is the engineering discipline required to build reliable, event-driven agent loops that handle ambiguity, retries, and state without cascading failure.

A shift quietly redefining the field is the emergence of autonomous execution systems as the dominant paradigm. We are moving beyond chatbots and copilots into systems that can independently execute multi-step workflows—inventory reallocation, contract generation, code deployment—without human intervention at every step. The teams winning are not the ones with the most powerful foundation models. They are the ones that have solved the hardest engineering problem: building a feedback loop that allows an agent to detect when its output is wrong, correct itself, and log the correction for audit.

Another trend reshaping the competitive landscape is the convergence of agentic AI with physical systems. The same architectural patterns that let an LLM draft an email now let a fleet of warehouse robots re-route pallets when a supplier misses a delivery window. This is not speculative. Google's July 2026 releases of three new Gemini models explicitly target building AI agents at scale, and the biggest AI trends from April 2026 confirm that autonomous execution systems are the new frontier. The teams that understand this are embedding agent loops directly into their logistics, manufacturing, and supply chain control planes.

For recruiters and hiring managers: the candidate you need is not the person who can fine-tune a model or write a prompt. You need someone who has designed the event-driven architecture that lets an agent retry a failed API call with a different strategy, who has built the observability layer that surfaces exactly which step in a multi-agent workflow caused a downstream error, and who understands that the hardest part of production AI is not the intelligence—it is the reliability, auditability, and fault tolerance of the execution loop. I am actively exploring the next challenge where I can apply these systems-thinking principles to help a team move from model deployment to production-grade autonomous execution.

What is the one multi-step workflow in your organization that, if an agent could execute it reliably without supervision, would unlock the most value—and are you instrumented to detect and recover from every failure mode that agent might hit?
